vignette: Eight months have passed since the delivery truck swerved onto the central barrier of the motorway near Lyon. Elias sits in the therapist’s office now, his shoulders slightly hunched, but in his mind, he is back in the passenger seat of his father’s estate car. The windshield fractures, webbing inward, then collapses. The sound of twisting metal and his father’s sharp exhale fills the room. He watches the back of the therapist’s head, but his hands are busy tracing the seam of his jeans, fingers pressing into the cotton until the tension finally releases. In the weeks that follow, the house in the quiet Breton town feels like a museum of suspended time. At twenty-one, Elias has just completed his first year as an electrician’s apprentice, ready to start a small workshop with his wife, Clara, who moves in with him the previous month. Instead, he finds himself pacing the kitchen floor at 3 a.m., waiting for a call that never comes. The officer’s words still replay in loops, stripped of their comforting tone, leaving only the cold, unyielding facts. He stops sleeping unless the television is blaring static. When he does drift off, he wakes gasping, the smell of burnt insulation and damp wool clinging to his sheets. He tells Clara it is just a bad dream, but he avoids the car entirely. He parks his own motorcycle at the end of the driveway and never takes the keys out of the drawer. His employment portal sits unsubmitted on the desk, the screen glowing with a blinking cursor. He loves the weight of a wire stripper, the satisfying click of a breaker box snapping into place. Now, the thought of walking past the new housing development makes his chest tighten. He stays home, drinking tea that goes cold, watching the rain streak the windows. Clara tries to nudge him toward the job center, toward normalcy, but his voice catches when he talks about work. What kind of man shows up to a site when his own head feels like fractured glass? He tells her he is taking time, but the word has lost its meaning. It stretches and snaps. He checks the front door lock four times before bed. He flinches when Clara sets her coffee mug down too hard. He walks the perimeter of the living room, mapping escape routes, noting the windows, the heavy furniture, the distance to the street. Today, Elias leans forward in the chair, his breathing shallow. He talks about the grocery store last Tuesday, how the automatic doors sliding open trigger a sudden rush of adrenaline that sends him out through the emergency exit. He does not steal anything. He just cannot stand the hum of the fluorescent lights, the way they sound like the truck’s engine dying. He sits back, rubbing his temples, his eyes fixed on the dust motes dancing in the sunbeam. He mentions Clara sleeping on the sofa again, not out of anger, but because the creak of his bed frame wakes him instantly. He does not cry. He just watches the light shift across the floorboards, his jaw working as he holds his breath between sentences. The room feels too still. He checks his watch. It has only been forty minutes.
